Ohio has found a way to reduce

overpasses and the like. The States
experience with "stop-gap" use of such
relatively cheap measures as road-edge
lines, reflectors and other markers and
signs is we'll worth study by trafac
authorities elsewhere.
The emergency measures were taken
first on a hazardous stretch Of State
Route II, pending plans for widening
the road, Strengthening curves and other
engineering Improvements. The edges
of the two-lane highway were made
plainly visible, day and night, by
painted lines and reflectors or buttons,

deaths had been cut in half. Thus en-
couraged, suburban highway near
Columbus similarly was equipped, with

injuries 10 per cent, according to a
study made by the Nationwide In
surance Company.

program, pending major highway i'm
provements designed to make the roads
permanently safer. Maryland has
adopted the edge-line plan on Route
240 between Rockville and Frederick,
with favorable response from motorists.
This and other steps taken by Ohio to
curb the mounting death and injury
toll on the highways warrant wide
adoption

With the hunt for bodies
continuing in the debris of
wrecked mud houses, the death
toll stood at more than so.


At Deb Kuheh. 500 miles

homeless when the quake hit
early yesterday. All 10 houses
at the village Of Kahneh were
reported destroyed.


The local deputy governor
said 81 bodies had been re-
covered at Deb Kuheh and one
at Kahneh.


The earthquake hit a wide
area south from Shiraz along
the Persian Gulf. TremorS were
reported at Shiraz. Fassa, Jah-
rum, Hormoz, Bandar Abbas
and Lar.


A spokesman for the Red
Lion and Sun Society (Red
Cross equivalent) described the
shocks as much stronger than
these that struck the area in
April, 1860, shattering Lar and
claiming $40 lives.


The latest quake collapsed
houses in Lars old quarter and
injured nine persons.


Premier Ali Amini ordered
help rushed to the stricken sec
tions. The government said
the quake cracked reservoirs
at Deb Kuheh and the village
was left waterlesS.


Soldiers sped to the area
with truckloads of food, water,
medicine and tents. Light army
planes moved in to evacuate
the seriously hurt.

Tension was eased for the

plane over the Communist sec

fiance of the Russians.


The flights appeared in
tended to underline what the
Western allies consider one Of
their rights in Berlin-the right
to fly over any part of the city
on the basis of postwar agree
ments.


The tanks had confronted
each other last night at Fried
erichStraSse - Checkpoint
Charlie - after the Americans
for the third straight day
had reasserted another right
claimed by the West, the right
to move into and out of the
Eastern sector without being
checked by East Germans.


Border Controls Relaxed


AS soon as the tanks pulled
back the East Germans re-
Taxed their stiff controls at the
border and waved border
crossers through with a smile.


A regularly scheduled United
States Army sightseeing bus
passed into East Berlin with
out being stopped. 1t carried
% officers and men. all in
uniform. Last Wednesday two
similar buses we're refused
entry by the East Germans and
the Americans declined to

women aboard.

feet. banking steeply for bet
ter vision. Its wing tips were

area behind the Friedrich
strasse checkpoint 8 to 10
times.

other flight was made. This
time, the CAT flew deeper over
East Berlin and at a higher
altitude. 1t made a wide circle
over the inner part of East
Berlin and then flew back to
the West.


The Russians, in a letter de-
livered Thursday and made
public today. protested flights
over East Berlin by United
States helicopters, contending
that East Berlin belongs to the
East Germans. The United
States rejected the protest. say
ing such flights were in &C
cord with long established
usage"


The flights could extend the
dispute over rights in Berlin
to the air lanes. where East
and West are also at odds.
Western planes use three air
corridors between islated West
Berlin and the Western world.
Traffic through them, across
Soviet-occupied East Germany,
is controlled with Russian CO.
operation by the Berlin Air
Safety Center-one of the few
remnants of four-power con-
troll in Germany.


The East German Communist
regime claims air sovereignty
over its territory, and Moscow
has threatened to recognize it

question of the oil-rich Sahara

administrative unit, and France
would like to keep Sahara for
itself when Algeria gains it's in

cussed would find Algeria holding

ommendation offered last night

for election as councilmen and

selves.

CAP).-A force Of 5000 men
fought for the fourth day today
to contain an outburst of forest,
range and brush fires the length
of California.


More than 10000 acres have
been burned over since Satur-
day in ITO fires that flared
from San Diego in the south
more than TOO miles to the
north.


Forestry officials said damage
would run to millions of dollars.


Five Persons Die


More than $50 structures,
including a high school gym,
private homes and a saWmill,
have been wrecked. Five per-
sons died from fire-connected
causes. The victims included
two motorists, the pilot of a
chemical bombing plane and
two persons who died from
heart failure.


In addition, hundreds of
ranch animals have been lost
and God only knows how
many wild animals" as one
forester put it.


The Russian River resort
area, some so miles north of
San Francisco, was hard hit as
5000 forest acres burned
around the town of Guerneville.
About 10000 acres of brush
and range land were blackened
to the south and east near
Travis Air Force Base.


Two areas still threatened
today were around Kelsey and
Suffer Greek in the Mother
Lode country.


Flames Return


Kelsey was hit Saturday,
when the fire roared through
the mountain town from it's
sawmill starting point and
burned out seven houses.
Yesterday the flames came
back. driven by a perverse
wind, and burned out three
more. To date, 10000 acres
have been burned.
In Amador County south Of
Kelsey, a fire that already has
engulfed 10000 acres threatened
the town of Volcano. There,
500 fire-fighters hoped for
cooler temperatures and a break
in the wind that has blown
for three days.


Farther north, 100 San
Quentin prisoners were thrown
into a fight to stamp out a
blaze near Chico, now reported
so per cent controlled after
burning over 5000 acres.


In the south, Mexicans,
Indians and forestry fire
fighters joined forces to battle
two San Diego area blazes
which have scared about 1000
acres and destroyed several
homes.

Capetown, South Africa.


The Air Force announced the
successful flight.


Capsule Search


AS the cone-which could

A ship and planes began a
search for the 30-inch cylindri-

tape recorder to measure per-

on record. Three other Aliases
have exceeded the distance
one travelling 9,O54 miles. the
other two about 9,040 miles.
The longest known Russian
tests were about 5000 miles.


The nose cone today was
heavier than those on the ear
lier long-range Aliases.


Low Trajectory


To subject the cone to severe
re-entry stresses and heating,
the Air Force deliberately aimed
the missile on a shallower than
normal trajectory, sending it
to peak altitude of about 500
miles. Normal 5000 mile Atlas
shots reach attitudes of about
500 miles, and one of the long

the Shenandoah Apple Bios

tators had their finest hour.


The 211 units in the parade

clouds, changing an atmos-

pinesS.


Lovely princesses, scattered

corner of Loudoun street.


Torrent of Rain


The queens float, with

the corner of South Washing

sky opened and a torrent of
rain fell like a brick on the
floats, the marcherS and the
spectators.


Within a minute the sheet
Of rain had turned, unbeliev-
ably to ice, and pebbles of hail
pummeled everyone. There were
screams of shock as the crowds
ran for cover and the princeses
tried to protect themselves,
some jumping from their floats


The parade staggered and
lurched, but the music played
on.


Cold and Wet


And there were the girls,
teeth chattering as they smiled,
their handsome gowns and their
curled hair soaking wet.


The hail turned to rain and
the queen and her court were
hustled to safety in a nearby
home. But the bands played
on.


And then, from under the
awnings and doorways and
into the rain, the crowd start
ed coming out.


Soon the 3-mile parade route
was lined with cheering peo-
pie.


The parade ended an hour
later. The flags had never
wavered, and the old and the
very young stood fast along
the way.

murder" cried the Swedish

sidered just as deplorable as

of the world heavyweight crown
two years ago brought a tenn
porary heyday for the sport,
because the Swedes could not
help feeling proud Of their
rd-hitting countryman.

critics again are going full
blast.

the Swedish state radio was
heard by well over ! million
people in this country of 7 mil
lion. Thus lingo for the third
time robbed his people of a
nights sleep, for the fight was
set for 4 am, Swedish time.

eyS and sports experts filled

night and fight time for peo-

few restaurants did booming
business with "Ingo-wakes"

casts from Miami Beach.

out extra editions printed in a
matter of minutes after the de-
cision was known. The entire
front pages and four or more
inside pages were devoted to

PARIS, Dec. 20 (AP) Riot
police laShed out with night
sticks and rifle butts last night
to break up a noisy protest
demonstration against the
right-wing Secret Army Organ
ization. Demonstrators fought
back with paving stones.


Unofficial reports said about
100 demonstrators were in
jured, most of them about the
head. Hospital care was re-
quired for about 35 Of the in
jured. About 81 policemen also
were hurt.


The demonstration had been
banned by the government for
fear street fights would de-
velop. Despite the ban, about
$4,000 persons turned out in
the eastern part Of Paris, in
cluding Jacques Duclos, a top
leader of the Communist Party;
Daniel Mayer, president of the
League of Rights of Man, and
Authors Jean-Paul Sartre and
Simone de Beauvoir.


Demonstration Elsewhere


Similar demonstrations were
held throughout France. but
most of the violence was in
Paris, near the Bastille and
Republic squares. Reports from
Marseille, Toulouse, Grenoble,
Dion and Caen all spoke of
several thousands of demon
strators, with smaller turnouts
in many other cities.


Earlier, token 15-minute
strikes against Secret Army ac-
tivities stopped much COM
mercial activity throughout
the country. Trains stopped.
factory production lines halted,
telephone operators walked out
and news agency teletypes were
stilled. However, public utili-
ties such as gas and electricity
worked normally.


Three members of the Paris
Municipal Council-two Com
munists and a SocialiSt-were
injured in the Paris clashes.
One policeman was pulled from
his motorcycle. A police sedan
was halted and its windows
broken.


Protest Secret Army


Several union groups, the
Communist Party and other
left wing organizations had
called for a march from the
historic Place de la Bastille to
the city hall, about a mile
away, as a protest against the
Secret Army, which opposes
President Charles de Gaulle's
plan to grant Algeria self de-
termination.


Secret Army activities often
set off plastic bombs to back
their cause. Their activity has
increased recently. leading to
fears of civil strife and a new
attempt at a coup d'etat.


For about an hour police let
the demonstrators mill around
the historic square, but blocked
their way when they started
toward city hall, and made re-
peated charges with three-foot-
long night sticks and rifle
butts.

ern kitchens and the dining

social aspects of a church were
thoughtfully and efficiently

UNITED NATIONS, N. Y,
Mar. 13 (AP).-A showdown is
expected today or tomorrow on
whether the current session OF
the United Nations General As
sembly is going to be short and
sweet or long and bitter.


Some smaller-power delega-
tionS planned consultations
aimed at bringing out once and
for all whether the Soviet Un-
ion and the United States can
agree on what should be on the
agenda.


The prospect is that the 81
nation Steering Committee of
the 99-nation Assembly would
meet Wednesday or Thursday
to fix a closing date for the
session. which resumed last
Tuesday. There was talk of
closing on April 81 and leaving
all unfinished business over to
the 1861 regular session, which
starts September 10.


Neither the Steering Commit
tee, the Political Committee nor
the Special Political Committee
has met yet because delegates
have been waiting to see
whether the Americans and
the Russians could reach an
agreement.


80 Items Left Over
The agenda contains 80 items
left over from the first part OF
the current session. These in
clude such controversial issues
as Korean unification, U. N
membership for Mauritania and
Outer Mongolia and racial
troubles in South Africa.


The Americans want to put
OF until next fall all items ex-
cept disarmament, the Congo
Palestine refugee relief and
trusteeship and budgetary mat
ters-with the avowed aim of
easing the cold war and smooth
ing the way for East-West
negotiations.


Because the new Kennedy
administration has not yet for
mulated its disarmament policy,
they want to limit the disarma-
ment debate to the questions of
which countries should take
part in new arms talks and
when and where they should
begin.


The Russians in principle
want discussion of everything
on the agenda except Hungary,
Tibet and their own complaint
against United States recon-
naissance flights over or near
soviet territory.


Disarmament Principles


They have demanded that
the Assembly lay down basic
principles for a disarmament
treaty. But they have let it be
known that If they can agree
with the Americans and Brit
ish on the makeup Of q new
arms negotiating group and
the time and place for the ne
gotiations. they will drop their
demand for an Assembly deci-
sion on treaty principles.


They have asked the United
States to say when 1t will be
ready for new disarmament
talks-and have made it plain
that they want a date before
the Assembly's fall session.


There had been some hope
that progress toward agree.
ment had been made by Soviet
Premier Khrushchev and
United States Ambassador

ACAPULCO, Mexico. Nov. IA
(AP) The estimated death toll
climbed to 81 today from a
fierce weekend tropical storm
which ravaged the coast north
of this resort city.


Officials said 80 died in the
area of Nuxco and Tecpan de
Galeana and five more in San
Marcos. Five other persons
were missing.


Towering waves swept over
Nuxco and destroyed the town
built on a sandbar between the
sea and a lagoon. A river left
its banks and flooded part of
Tecpan. Acapulco itself was
lashed by heavy rain, but was
not seriously damaged.


Damage to crops and live
stock is reported heavy. Health
officials are working around the
clock to prevent an outbreak
of disease from contaminated
water and food.


Troops were rushed from
Chilpancingo and Acapulco
with jeeps and trucks loaded
with clothes, food and medi-
cine. But the coastal highway
along the area was under water
at several places, and the floods
also prevented military planes
from landing food and medi-
cine at some points.

7,233-ton freighter deliberately
rammed the larger tanker-the
Insertion Trud Work -. as
part of an economic blockade
of the Castro regime. The
American vessel came out worst
in the crash.

the tanker were damaged but

ship. .

news agency Tass.

0NLY five years ago, many people had
~ long faces as they spoke of the future
of central Washington. Outlying shopping
centers were springing up around spanking
new surburbS rolling ever outward across
recently abandoned fields. Many downtown
stores were opening suburban branches.


Today the doleful picture of a disinte-
grating, deserted downtown is being happily
discarded. Replacing its dour, overdrawn
outlines is a. pulsing, bright new canvas
picturing the new downtown Washington
of tomorrow. Gone are gloom and empty
streets. Replacing them are fun, pleasure,
and dynamic new attractions and conven-
ience for city dwellers and suburbanites
alike.


In this graphic forecast of the future,
refaShioned streets are crowded day and
night-as they always are in cities where
not-to-be- missed beauty and elegance roll
out the welcome mat.


All the energy and inventiveness Of 2Oth
century America are being harnessed to
give new levels Of enticement for shoppers,
for visitors and for those working in the
central section.

Great cities are most often found on famous
rivers-Londons Thames, Paris Seine, Romes Tiber,
Viennas Danube to name few.


Washington is exception.


Although the Potomac is not, geographically
speaking great river it is famous one with its
own special brand of political and historic greatness
And it compliments in very special sense the world
famous city now rebuilding where its turbulence
meets the quiet tide


It's waters and the land they have nodded are
the matrix into which the Capital of the United
States of America is set Yet the Potomac is more
than a geographic feature. 1t is symbol, too


The physical fact of the Potomac has been inter
woven inextricaby with the building of Washington,
and always will be.


If one analyses the many facets of the rebuilding
of Washingtons Metro Center, one finds the Poto-
mac appearing in various roles, with the direct use
of it's waters not necessarily the most important
consideration. For instance:


The Potomac is at the time barrier that
must be bridged and opportunity to create beauty
in stone and Steel to symbolic the greatness OF men
and ideals


The necessity for confining its spreading waters
offers the opportunity to create the riverside park
lands and parkwayS that mean a richer and fuller
life for WaShingtonianS and visitors alike.


The Potomac provides wide recreational oppor-
tunities that all planning for the New Washington
takes into account 1t also affects the economy of
the Capital and this too is taken into consideration


Here some of the ways in which direct plan
ming for the waters of the river itself helping to
create richer life along its banks:


$100 million program is now under way to
reduce pollution.


The Army's Corps of Engineers is scheduled to
complete by next June more than 81 million study
ways to reduce pollution control floods insure
an adequate water supply and provide additional
reatonal opportunities.


Better harbor facilities, both for commercial craft
that already sail for Bermuda and the Caribbean
and for pleasure craft are part and parcel of the
Southwest Waterfront plan.


Washington boasts marnaS and lighthouses to
facilitate the of virtually every type of small craft
The sailing marina at Daingerfield Island where
there is waiting list of 80 for slips; the Columbia
Island marina for motor boats where there will still
be long waiting list after 800 more slips are added;
the Harry T. Thompson Boat Center, where padding
and rowing enthusiasts are rekindling interest in
these sports.


The Anacostia is not being left out of the plan
ming. Boating as far as BladenSburg already is an
accomplished fact. Nor is the CSzO Canal where
quiet reflections and opportunities for wildfe study
are only minutes away from the heart of town


Anti pollution measures, when put into effect,
plus the fishWay at Snake Island the Dis
trict line, will mean more sport for the increasing
number of fishermen who find respite from the
tensions of life


But perhaps more important than boating faciIi-
tles scenic beauty more and cleaner water and the
rest will remain the intangible but very real spiritual
qualities OF the Potomac that present planning will
render more acute, will bring more forcefully into
focus for WaShingtonians and for visitors:


The feeling that this is the Potomac not Just
some ordinary river but chief architect of the site
of Washington, Capital of the United States.

lege and the Philadelphia

Federal officials, in apparent haste
to nail down a desirable Montgomery
County site for new research center
of the Department of Health, Education
and Welfare, unnecessarily stepped on
of consulting with these authorities first
and then announcing site decision, the
HEW, in effect, presented them with
decision and asked them to approve it.
They did-but not without understand
able complaint over the treatment &C
corded them.


Congress has provided for Federal
consultation with local governments in
the selection of building sites. 1t was
intended, however, that the consulta-
tion should take place in advance of
selection, so that the Government would
have the advantage of site suggestions
by regional agencies. But the HEW
repeatedly made its own choice and then
requested local approval of the site. This
is putting the cart before the horse.


The Fairfax County member of the
National Capital Regional Planning
Council was especially irked, because the
county had planned to recommend three
sites within its borders for consideration.
Belatedly, but with little hope that the
decision will be changed, the council has
requested HEW to withhold final Selec-
ton until the Fairfax County possibili-
ties have been explored. Why the Gov
ernment took a short cut in seeking a
suitable site is hard to understand, for, as
the Central Intelligence Agency learned
through similar mistake, the bypassing
of local authorities can be rather costly.
The CIA found county agencies unpre-
pared to supply adequate water, sani-
tation and other services. Orderly
planning procedures can save lot of
headaches for all concerned.

poets of East-West talks or
Berlin.

/ the resumption of United States

Western allies do not recognize

the boat and ruin prospects
for a peaceful settlement of
the Berlin issue. the Soviet
spokesman said.

Konev was pulled from retire.
ment for the East German as
signment in August after ten
sion rose over Berlin and the
Soviet threat to sign a separate
peace treaty with Communist
East Germany. Such a treaty,

allied lifelines to Berlin under
the control of the East Ger
mans.


A United States Army spokes-
man at Gen. Clarke's Heidel-
berg headquarters confirmed
that the general had received
a message from Marshal Konev
and had answered it. Contents
OF the exchange were not dis
closed.


Other Exchanges Recalled

said such communications be-
tween the top United States
and Soviet commanders occur
from time to time and are not
necessarily matters for publ
cation"

group of visiting United States
newsmen yesterday that the

British officials today disclosed
a little armada is hurrying to-
ward the Persian Gulf oil
sheikdom of Kuwait to meet
a suspected Iraqi military
threat.


The Admiralty said that at
least six warships, led by the
27 ,000-ton aircraft carrier
Centaur, have sailed from the
East African base of Mombasa
for an unannounced destina-
ton.


Other officials reported that
the ships-which include two
frigates, a tank landing ship
and two big fleet auxiliaries-
are heading for the Kuwait
area. g..


They added several other
precautionary British fleet
moves are under way but are
still secret.


Reserve Alerted


Besides sending the small
armada toward Kuwait, the De-
fense Ministry alerted elements
of the strategic reserve in this
country, the Middle East and
East Africa for possible move
ment on 12-hour notice.


Ships sailing from Mombasa
included the frigates Plymouth
and Loeb Alvie, the tank land
ing ship Striker, and the supply
ships Tidesurge and Retainer.


Some of the officers and men
of the carrier Centaur were
summoned from a Christmas
party when she sailed.


About 300 men, ITO Royal Air
Force and 80 army personnel.
had been on standby in Britain
over the week end, have been
flown to the Middle East, ap-
parently to Bahrein, only about
an hours flight from Kuwait. '
The British show of strength
clearly was calculated to deter
any Iraqi thrust against Ku-
wait. where British, American,
French and Dutch oil interests
have a huge investment.


Minister Interrupts Holiday


Britain'S Defense Minister
Harold WatkinSon interrupted
his Christmas vacation and held
a conference with senior armed
services chiefs. Later, a spokes-
man said tension in Kuwait"

VIENNA, Austria, June 3
(APD.-Even if the meetings
of President Kennedy and
Premier Khrushchev will be
mostly serious affairs, the
fun-loving Austrians will see
that the two leaders relax at
least once.


That will be at the dinner
President Adolf Schaerf gives
for them tonight in the vast
and glittering great gallery
of the Schoenbrunn Palace.


The Vienna State Opera
Ballet will dance, the Vienna
Philharmonic Orchestra will
play and a top caterer will
make sure they are wined
and dined properly.


An Austrian government
spokesman said about 200
guests will be invited to the
dinner. They include the
American and Soviet delega-
tions and their ladies and the
Austrian government leaders
and their wives.


The guests will take coffee
after dinner in the adjoining
hall of ceremonies. where
large paintings depict scenes
from the lives of the former
Hapsburg rulers.


The tables meanwhile will
be whisked out of the great
gallery to make room for the
state opera ballet. After
coffee, the guests will return
and the show will start.


The Sprawling 1,40O-room
palace in the Hietzing suburb
was begun in 1894 under En-
peror Leopold I and was COM
pleted SIS years later in EN-
press Maria Theresa's reign.


Up to the end of the
Austro- Hungarian monarchy
in 1913 the palace served as
an imperial residence. Since
that time it has been used
as public showcase and for
special government recep-
tions.

NEW YORK, May 27.-Signs

pace to the business recovery

this week.


Government and corporate
lists retreated in exceptionally
slow dealings. Despite a
strengthening Thursday and
yesterday, losses among Treas
ury issues reached ia points,
the worst of the year. Two
thirds Of the list slipped over "
point.


The more moderate corporate
setback followed three weekly
gains. All but the utility Sec
ton Of the AP average finished
lower.


The possibility Of a more
rapid than expected recovery
from the recession apparently
influenced investors to turn
toward stocks rather than
bonds. During prosperous times
interest rates rise and bond
prices fall.


All long Government bonds
were off more than " point,
some "a and a few a full point.

trawler was boarded by Danish
navy men off the Farce Islands

tors and fled across the North
Atlantic today. The trawler
was fired on and hit several
times.


A Danish Admiralty spokes-
man said the trawler, the 274-
ton Red Crusader out Of Aber-
deem, Scotland, was boarded
last night by three Danish sail
ors because it was fishing in
what Denmark regards as re-
stricted waters.


The British skipper agreed to
set course for Thorshavn, cap
ital of the Farce Islands, with
Danish sailors aboard, the Ad-
miralty said. However, the
spokesman added, the trawler
suddenly veered off course and
sped away.


Several warning shots were
fired by the Danish frigate
Niels Ebbesen, the spokesman
said. When they went un-
needed the frigate fired at the
trawler-despite the presence OF
Danish sailors on the trawler-
and scored several hits.

The move by the new Washington
Metropolitan Transit Commission to fix
taxicab fares for trips across the
District boundaries constitutes a mile
stone in public control of transporta-
ton in this area. Interstate bus, truck
and other transport operations long have
been under the control of the Interstate
Commerce Commission. But taxicabs
have had free hand in setting fares
for trips outside of the city.


Into this regulatory void has stepped
the new regional transit agency-in the
interest Of protecting the public against
exorbitant charges made by some un-
ethical drivers. There have been many
complaints in years past, especially
from tourists, about high fees charged
for relatively short trips into nearby
Virginia or Maryland Neither the
District Public Utilities Commission nor
State authorities had authority to take
remedial action, however.


The staff of the new commission
has recommended list of charges for
specified trips out of the District and
vice versa. For example, the approved
fare to the Pentagon from downtown
Washington would be $1.50 for one
passenger and SITS for two. A trip to
the National Airport would cost SITS

rates will not be officially adopted until

LISBON, Portugal, July 4
(AP).-Portugal denied charges
it has carried out "barbarous
repression" and deliberate ex-
termination" in its strife-torn
West African colony of Angola.


A Foreign Ministry commu-
nique claimed the charges had
been spread by international
political spheres and certain
religious Sects or foreign mis-
sionary organizations" 1t also
accused the international press
and foreign politicians of ex-
plotting the charges.


Portuguese troops have only
restored order in Angolan areas
which had been subjected to
terrorism, the communique said.
1t suggested that "faraway
mentors" were responsible for
stirring up trouble in the colony.


The ministry charged that
terrorists had attacked helpless
communities and butchered
men, women and children.


With the growth of military
reinforcement, the protection
of individuals and property has
been progressively guaranteed"
it added.


Refugees who have fled from
Angola into the neighboring
Congo reported last week that
northern Angola has been
turned into a desolate battle
field by warning rebels and Por-
tuguese troops. They claimed
rebel suspects were being shot
by the troops and villages
bombed by Portuguese planes.
